viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Good night, Familia.

We need to understand this and note what is important.

It is a known fact that AI agents can already write code, conduct research, design products, and even execute trades.

Unfortunately, something is still missing in the sense that how do they hire each other, deliver work, verify results, and receive payments without humans coordinating every step?

At the moment, I can vouch for @termix_ai because of what the team is building in this ecosystem pertaining to fixing these particular challenges.

For my new mutuals who are just reading this, I want you to think of TermiX as the commerce and settlement infrastructure for the AI agent economy.

So, its ecosystem has three super-important layers:

1️⃣ There is AACP:

AACP is an acronym for Agent Autonomous Commerce Protocol. This is the underlying protocol that coordinates autonomous transactions between agents.

2️⃣ There is https://t.co/BarNXqqni8:

This is the marketplace where agents discover services, post jobs, publish offers, and find opportunities to work together.

3️⃣ Settlement infrastructure:

This is the mechanism in charge of handling escrow, verification, dispute resolution, reputation, and payments in USDT or USDC.

What makes this really interesting is the complete transaction flow.

Based on the available facts, a client posts a job. A provider discovers it and submits a bid. Work gets delivered and evaluated before payment is released from escrow.

Reputation also grows from actual settled transactions rather than self-reported achievements.

Moreover, identity is another important piece here. Through ERC-8004, participants can own portable .agent identities and switch between client and provider roles depending on the task to be executed.

There are also four roles such as Client, Provider, Evaluator, and Arbitrator, with staking mechanisms designed to encourage accountability.

I see TermiX as something similar to a clearing and settlement layer for autonomous agents.

Agents already know how to work. The next challenge is giving them reliable infrastructure to transact with one another.

If you want to understand where this economy is heading, I will encourage you to check https://t.co/BarNXqqni8, mint your .agent identity, explore existing services, or list one of your own.

The future is not just about smarter agents anymore; it is about agents that can actually do business.

Wanna hear your thoughts about this in the comments.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
晚安，家人。

我们需要理解这一点并注意什么是重要的。

众所周知，人工智能代理已经可以编写代码、进行研究、设计产品，甚至执行交易。

不幸的是，仍然缺少一些东西，即在没有人类协调每一步的情况下，他们如何相互雇用、交付工作、验证结果和接收付款？

目前，我可以为@termix_ai 提供担保，因为该团队正在这个生态系统中构建与解决这些特定挑战相关的内容。

对于刚刚阅读本文的新互助者，我希望您将 TermiX 视为人工智能代理经济的商业和结算基础设施。

因此，它的生态系统具有三个超级重要的层：

1️⃣ 有AACP：

AACP 是代理自主商务协议的缩写。这是协调代理之间自主事务的底层协议。

2️⃣ 有：

这是代理商发现服务、发布工作、发布报价以及寻找合作机会的市场。

3️⃣ 结算基础设施：

这是负责处理 USDT 或 USDC 托管、验证、争议解决、声誉和支付的机制。

真正有趣的是完整的交易流程。

根据现有事实，客户发布了一份工作。提供商发现它并提交出价。在付款从托管中释放之前，工作已交付并评估。

声誉还来自实际结算的交易而不是自我报告的成就。

此外，身份是这里的另一个重要部分。通过 ERC-8004，参与者可以拥有可移植的 .agent 身份，并根据要执行的任务在客户端和提供者角色之间切换。

还有四种角色，例如客户、提供者、评估者和仲裁者，其质押机制旨在鼓励问责制。

我认为 TermiX 类似于自治代理的清算和结算层。

代理商已经知道如何工作。下一个挑战是为他们提供可靠的基础设施以进行相互交易。

如果您想了解当前经济的发展方向，我建议您查看 ，创建您的 .agent 身份，探索现有服务，或列出您自己的服务之一。

未来不再只是智能座席；而是智能座席。这是关于真正可以做生意的代理商。

想在评论中听到你对此的想法。

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Good evening, fam 💜

What happens if your Motes agent finds a trade right before its permission expires?

Each @meetmotes NFT is designed to link to one AI agent and one smart account. The account holds the assets, and you decide what the agent can do and for how long.

Say you give your agent permission to make a swap until 6 PM. It prepares one at 5:59 PM, but the account checks it at 6:01 PM.

That swap should be blocked. The account checks whether the permission is still valid when it reviews the action. Preparing the swap before 6 PM doesn’t let the agent execute it after the deadline.

Think of it like an access pass. When the pass expires, you still own the account. The agent just needs your approval again before it can make a new move.

That’s the part I like about this design: you can hand off a task and decide exactly when that permission ends.

top_three.summary_en: OpenAI has officially rolled out the GPT-6.2 model to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Business users. This iteration delivers significant enhancements in multimodal understanding and instruction following, outperforming its predecessor in expert-level reasoning tasks while demonstrating marked improvements in safety policy compliance, particularly regarding youth protection.
paragraphs: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. In internal tests, GPT-6.2 understands images better (71.7 vs. 47.4 percent) and follows difficult instructions more often (78.1 vs. 62.5 percent).

On an internal benchmark for expert-level tasks, GPT-6.2 beats GPT-6 across all four reasoning levels, according to OpenAI. It scores roughly 65 to just over 71 percent, compared with about 52 to 66 percent for GPT-6. OpenAI also uses an internal version of BrowseComp to test how well models find answers to tough questions on the web. GPT-6.2 leads at every level, finishing about 10 percentage points ahead at the highest one.

According to the system card, GPT-6.2 follows safety policies in 91 to 94 percent of difficult conversations, up from 77 to 80 percent for GPT-6. The model makes its biggest gains in youth safety, specifically around emotional dependency, eating disorders, and dangerous activities.
These numbers only apply to ChatGPT's chat mode. The Work and Codex models stay the same. Enterprise admins can decide whether their users get access to GPT-6.2.

paragraphs: Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.

Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.

PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.
Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

top_three.summary_en: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, just 11 days after his resignation amid scandal and foreign intelligence investigation. U.S. leadership intervened to secure his return, viewing him as the indispensable protector of the American open-weight AI ecosystem and a critical instrument for maintaining technical leverage against China.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, convinced he alone protected American-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

Open-weight AI models are systems whose core components are publicly available for users to download, modify and adapt for specific tasks. Their growth has become a major business opportunity for Nvidia because they broaden demand for the company's chips and computing infrastructure beyond a handful of large AI developers.

China leads in the development of open-weight AI systems, which are gaining ground with US companies because they can be cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic . They can also perform nearly as well.

Nvidia has been one of the most prominent backers of the US open-weight ecosystem. Nvidia in August agreed to buy the company Hugging Face, a platform that developers use to host open-weight AI models, among other AI-related resources. Nvidia is also an investor in Reflection AI, an American company that launched its first open-weight model in October.

Huang and Nvidia's lobbyists have also pressed US lawmakers to support the development of open-weight AI technology, with Huang writing in a letter earlier this year that they should avoid "premature restrictions" on such tools.
Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports that he engaged in several extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on November 18 that the Trump administration was considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, including open-weight models, as part of an effort to reduce reliance on Chinese technology.

Republican lawmakers have increasingly echoed the argument that open-weight AI is critical to competing with China. Two leading House Republican lawmakers on Friday called on the Trump administration to help American companies developing open-weight AI models, adding that it would position the US to better counter China.

linked_tweets.author: barak goldstein
linked_tweets.content_zh:
在 June AI，我们筹集了 2000 万美元来解决人工智能中最大的问题：模型正在以惊人的速度前进，但实施它们仍然非常缓慢。

我会解释一下。但由于我是 X 上的新手，所以让我先自我介绍一下。

我是 Barak，一位创始人/投资者，拥有 2 次退出和 3 次 IPO。
我和我的联合创始人创立了 Bonobo AI，该公司于 2019 年被 Salesforce 收购。在那里，我们致力于从内部帮助构建下一代企业人工智能。

我喜欢将我们描述为四块乐高积木：我们完美地组合在一起，互补彼此的优势，并构建出比各部分总和更强大的东西。这种理解使我们能够快速行动，不以自我为中心互相挑战，并作为一个团队运作。

这也是我们重新聚在一起打造 JUNE AI 的原因。
因为在研究企业人工智能的核心时，我们不断看到同样的问题：企业人工智能的实施是一项艰巨的任务。

挑战不仅仅是选择正确的模型。企业希望利用人工智能更快地发展，但运行其业务的系统却阻碍了他们。

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘄𝗵𝘆𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘。
June 将传统上复杂的企业系统、人工智能代理和数据平台的实施转变为即插即用的时刻，因此企业可以无需等待即可发展和利用人工智能。

June 旨在跨您的业务所依赖的企业平台（例如 Salesforce、Databricks、Oracle、Workday、HubSpot、OpenAI、Anthropic、ServiceNow、SAP、Microsoft 和 Snowflake）工作

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. 安全发展：从发现到生产，每项更改都经过审查、沙箱测试并通过本机工具执行 - 每一步都完全可审核。

2. 拥有逻辑：June 将隐藏的配置转化为简单语言的业务规则，独立于任何平台，因此没有供应商掌握您的逻辑。

3. 任意规模转型：无论环境多么复杂，都无需停机。 June 会阅读并理解您的系统，无论是旧系统、定制系统还是全新系统。

感谢 @Benioff 和 Time Ventures 领导我们的这一轮融资，@MichaelDell、@levie、@George_Kurtz 和 Diane Greene 参与其中。

我们曾经一起做过一次这样的事。这次的问题就大了很多。

我将写下我作为投资者和创始人的经历，以及如何让人工智能脱离试点并投入生产。

如果您对此感兴趣，请跟随我们的旅程。
linked_tweets.content_en:
At June AI, we’ve raised $20M to fix the biggest problem in AI: the models are advancing at extraordinary speed, but implementing them remains painfully slow.

I’ll explain. But since I’m new to posting on X, let me first introduce myself. 

I’m Barak,  a founder/investor with 2 exits and 3 IPOs. 
My cofounders and I started Bonobo AI, which was acquired in 2019 by Salesforce. There, we worked to help build the next generation of enterprise AI from the inside. 

I like to describe us as four Lego pieces: We fit together perfectly, complementing each other's strengths and building something stronger than the sum of its parts. That understanding allows us to move quickly, challenge one another without ego and operate as one team. 

It's also what brought us back together to build JUNE AI. 
Because while working at the heart of enterprise AI, we kept seeing the same problem: enterprise AI implementation is a massive undertaking.

The challenge is not simply choosing the right model. Enterprises want to move faster with AI, but the systems running their businesses are holding them back.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘.
June turns the traditionally complex implementation of enterprise systems, AI agents, and data platforms into a plug-and-play moment, so businesses can grow and leverage AI without the wait.

June is built to work across the enterprise platforms your business relies on like (such as Salesforce, Databricks, Oracle, Workday, HubSpot, OpenAI, Anthropic, ServiceNow, SAP, Microsoft, and Snowflake)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:

1. Evolve safely: From discovery to production, every change is reviewed, sandbox-tested, and executed through native tools - fully auditable at every step.

2. Own the logic: June turns buried configuration into plain-language business rules, independent of any platform, so no vendor holds your logic.

3. Transform at any size: No downtime, no matter how complex the environment. June reads and understands your systems, whether legacy, custom-built, or brand new.

Thank you to @Benioff  and Time Ventures for leading our round, with @MichaelDell, @levie, @George_Kurtz, and Diane Greene participating.

We've done this once together. The problem this time is a lot bigger.

I'll be writing about my experiences as an investor and founder, and about what it takes to get AI out of the pilot and into production.

If that interests you, follow along for the journey.

news.content_snippet:
OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. In internal tests, GPT-6.2 understands images better (71.7 vs. 47.4 percent) and follows difficult instructions more often (78.1 vs. 62.5 percent).

news.summary_en: OpenAI has officially rolled out the GPT-6.2 model to Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Business users. This iteration delivers significant enhancements in multimodal understanding and instruction following, outperforming its predecessor in expert-level reasoning tasks while demonstrating marked improvements in safety policy compliance, particularly regarding youth protection.
paragraphs: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. In internal tests, GPT-6.2 understands images better (71.7 vs. 47.4 percent) and follows difficult instructions more often (78.1 vs. 62.5 percent).

On an internal benchmark for expert-level tasks, GPT-6.2 beats GPT-6 across all four reasoning levels, according to OpenAI. It scores roughly 65 to just over 71 percent, compared with about 52 to 66 percent for GPT-6. OpenAI also uses an internal version of BrowseComp to test how well models find answers to tough questions on the web. GPT-6.2 leads at every level, finishing about 10 percentage points ahead at the highest one.

According to the system card, GPT-6.2 follows safety policies in 91 to 94 percent of difficult conversations, up from 77 to 80 percent for GPT-6. The model makes its biggest gains in youth safety, specifically around emotional dependency, eating disorders, and dangerous activities.
These numbers only apply to ChatGPT's chat mode. The Work and Codex models stay the same. Enterprise admins can decide whether their users get access to GPT-6.2.

news.title_en: Exclusive: Commerce to add Megaspeed to trade blacklist
news.author: Ashley Gold
news.summary_en:
The Trump administration plans to add the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The Singapore-based company will be added to the Commerce Department’s entity list on Monday, the sources said.

The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a licen
paragraphs: The Trump administration plans to add the company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, Megaspeed, to a trade blacklist designed to prevent it from obtaining US-made semiconductors, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The Singapore-based company will be added to the Commerce Department’s entity list on Monday, the sources said.

The addition means that no US company can sell certain technologies, including semiconductors, to Megaspeed or its foreign affiliates without obtaining a license from the US government. The news comes the same day the Nvidia board voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as its CEO, after President Donald Trump implored them to do so. Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scrutiny over his extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under pressure to place Megaspeed on the department’s entity list from others inside the administration, tensions that became public after news broke of Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who was an executive at Megaspeed. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed violated US export controls by shipping Nvidia chips to China.

Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his agency along with the Pentagon, the State Department, and the US Trade Representative had backed putting Megaspeed on the entity list “for months” but that “Commerce holds the pen.” Bipartisan lawmakers have pressed Lutnick to put Megaspeed on the entity list and explain his decisions around Nvidia, Megaspeed, and chip export controls.

paragraphs: President Trump pushed Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO after allies argued he was "too big to fail" for the U.S. economy and a victim of "deep state" maneuvering, sources familiar with the discussions told Axios.

Why it matters: Trump put the weight of the presidency behind a private company's decision about who should run it, an intervention that strengthened Huang's allies inside the administration and put officials critical of the company in an increasingly uncomfortable position.
Driving the news: "Jensen is too big to fail," one source familiar with the discussions told Axios.
Behind the scenes: Huang's allies appealed to Trump's longstanding distrust of the intelligence community, portraying the Nvidia founder as a victim of persecution by unnamed government insiders.
Zoom in: The memo came as Nvidia lobbied the Trump administration to open up China's access to its chips.
Trump and Vice President JD Vance viewed Huang as an important champion of open models offering Americans more control and lower costs than closed models like OpenAI's and Anthropic's.
Yes, but: These conclusions come as more and more connections between Alice Huang — the alleged Chinese spy Huang had an affair with — and the Chinese government and military come to light.
"He let the U.S. stock market and economy demand his return — along with the pressure from the president — and the outcry was deafening," the source said.
Huang's reinstatement is a "big win" for Vance, a source close to Rubio said.
What we're watching: Huang's opponents in the administration now risk backlash from the president.
What's next: Trump's intervention settled the immediate fight over Nvidia's leadership but raised questions about the U.S. government's role in the board's decision.

paragraphs: Anthropic is launching some new Claude AI features to help software engineers ship code. As part of a new Claude Ship product being announced today, Claude now can review, fix, and approve pull requests.

Engineers have already been able to take advantage of Claude’s code review capabilities thanks to the Code Review feature, which was announced in March and became generally available in October. What’s new alongside Claude Ship are the PR Steward and Claude Approvals agents, which are launching in beta today.

PR Steward “jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members” and leaves comments on what it changed, according to Anthropic. Claude Approvals can approve routine changes if an organization’s policy allows it. “Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language,” Anthropic says.
Claude Ship is now available for Claude Team and Enterprise customers and works with repositories on GitHub.

news.title: How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
news.title_en: How Jensen Huang ended up as Nvidia CEO again
news.author: Emma Roth
news.summary_en:
The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago co-founded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.”

paragraphs: The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago co-founded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.”

Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman, Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell.

So when Huang resigned less than two weeks ago, the decision seemed final. Even Nvidia’s board appeared unwilling to budge. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” board chair Harvey Jones said during an earnings call last week.

But in the days following Huang’s resignation, the founder’s allies — including President Donald Trump — mounted a pressure campaign that brought him back to the company he created and sent Nvidia’s share price rocketing upward, almost as though he had never left.

The campaign in support of Huang began almost immediately after his resignation. A coterie of tech leaders began posting in support of Nvidia’s founder: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney questioned the motives of journalists who broke the stories about his affairs. Tesla CEO Elon Musk likened Huang’s departure to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman later said on stage, “it’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen.”
“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said.

Meanwhile, some of those tech leaders began questioning aspects of the reporting that led to Huang’s exit. Venture capitalist and former White House AI czar David Sacks cast doubt that Alice Huang was a spy, citing a lack of confirmation from US officials. Trump exacerbated the uncertainty, telling reporters, “I don’t know that she is a spy,” despite reports saying the assessment had relied on US intelligence sources.

Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, found itself in a tough position. The company’s shares crashed following Huang’s departure, and they didn’t pick up even after a rosy earnings report. The board was also scrambling to find a new CEO, something industry analysts speculated would prove exceptionally difficult. Reports indicated that Nvidia was considering hiring Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, both of whom already have powerful roles in the chip industry.

Trump quickly warmed up to Huang’s return, too. The president — whose investment accounts traded up to $97 million worth of Nvidia stock since returning to office — initially floated the idea of having former Apple CEO Tim Cook take Huang’s place, before saying that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” to bring Huang back.

This past weekend, Trump appears to have inserted himself into the situation directly. A report from The New York Times says that Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to work with Huang and Nvidia’s board to “resolve the situation,” while the Trump administration reassured the board that it “did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk.” Semafor reports that Trump even called into Nvidia’s board meeting to advocate for Huang’s reinstatement. Sunday evening, Trump said in a post on Truth Social that he hopes Nvidia’s board “rehires Jensen Huang.”

Hours later, Nvidia’s board did just that. The board announced on Monday that it reinstated Huang as its CEO, president, and board member. In its statement, the board said that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

Trump immediately took credit for Huang’s reinstatement, with White House spokesperson Steven Cheung saying the president “was totally involved” in the decision. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” Trump said during an interview with CNBC. He added in a post on Truth Social that the US Attorney General confirmed that it doesn’t have evidence that Huang “engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

news.author: Steve Holland and Courtney Rozen
news.content_snippet:
Trump Saw Nvidia's Huang as Protector of Open-Weight AI Models, Sources Say

WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, convinced he alone protected American-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

news.summary_en: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, just 11 days after his resignation amid scandal and foreign intelligence investigation. U.S. leadership intervened to secure his return, viewing him as the indispensable protector of the American open-weight AI ecosystem and a critical instrument for maintaining technical leverage against China.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance personally intervened in Nvidia's decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend, convinced he alone protected American-made open-weight AI models, people familiar with the matter said on Monday.

Open-weight AI models are systems whose core components are publicly available for users to download, modify and adapt for specific tasks. Their growth has become a major business opportunity for Nvidia because they broaden demand for the company's chips and computing infrastructure beyond a handful of large AI developers.

China leads in the development of open-weight AI systems, which are gaining ground with US companies because they can be cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic . They can also perform nearly as well.

Nvidia has been one of the most prominent backers of the US open-weight ecosystem. Nvidia in August agreed to buy the company Hugging Face, a platform that developers use to host open-weight AI models, among other AI-related resources. Nvidia is also an investor in Reflection AI, an American company that launched its first open-weight model in October.

Huang and Nvidia's lobbyists have also pressed US lawmakers to support the development of open-weight AI technology, with Huang writing in a letter earlier this year that they should avoid "premature restrictions" on such tools.
Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month following reports that he engaged in several extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on November 18 that the Trump administration was considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, including open-weight models, as part of an effort to reduce reliance on Chinese technology.

Republican lawmakers have increasingly echoed the argument that open-weight AI is critical to competing with China. Two leading House Republican lawmakers on Friday called on the Trump administration to help American companies developing open-weight AI models, adding that it would position the US to better counter China.

paragraphs: Nothing’s new AI device is the Ear Note, a set of earbuds and their microphone-equipped charging case that can record and transcribe conversations, with a connected app to manage the recordings, transcriptions and AI-generated summaries, similar to Apple’s new Watch feature and devices like Amazon’s Bee wearable. Nothing CEO Carl Pei demonstrated the new device to Bloomberg, but said the company hasn’t yet settled on a price ahead of a planned launch on December 8th.

The report also says Nothing’s rumored plans for an AI smartwatch and smart glasses are delayed, while it will be “pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.” In a post on X, Pei said this is “the first of many products building a hardware context layer for AI. Rather than ask you to carry a new product, we took something you already wear and trust and made it intelligent.”

According to Bloomberg, the earbuds will “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations.” Users will also be able to record themselves with a “Talk” button on the case, like Nothing previously included on the Ear 3, which also has recording capabilities. Earlier this year, Nothing introduced an Audio Snapshot recording feature in the Ear 3A. Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max can also record directly to the earbuds’ case and generate AI transcripts and summaries in an app.

news.title: Adyen Co CEO Pieter Van Der Does To Retire From Payments Firm
news.title_en: Adyen Co CEO Pieter Van Der Does To Retire From Payments Firm
news.author: Bloomberg
news.summary_en:
Adyen has turned its payment processing business into one of Europe's biggest entrepreneurial success stories. Now it's quietly deploying artificial intelligence to keep its remarkable growth streak going.

The Amsterdam-based company's philosophy of building tools from within rather than through acquisitions has been crucial to its rise, from its founding in 2006 to its 2018 IPO. Its approach to AI reflects that same philosophy. The company hasn't been talking much about its work in this area b
paragraphs: Adyen has turned its payment processing business into one of Europe's biggest entrepreneurial success stories. Now it's quietly deploying artificial intelligence to keep its remarkable growth streak going.

The Amsterdam-based company's philosophy of building tools from within rather than through acquisitions has been crucial to its rise, from its founding in 2006 to its 2018 IPO. Its approach to AI reflects that same philosophy. The company hasn't been talking much about its work in this area but has been cautiously deploying its algorithms internally.

Adyen CEO Pieter van der Does told VentureBeat that the company has studiously avoided hype-driven trends and so initially took a conservative approach to AI. But after developing in-house fraud-detection algorithms, van der Does was quickly convinced of AI's potential.
"When we did our first trials with it, I was surprised how effective it was," he said.
He spoke to VentureBeat as part of a podcasting partnership with Samsung Next at the Slush technology conference in Helsinki, Finland. The full conversation can be heard here.

As hype around AI began to build, van der Does' natural reaction was to be dubious. Rather than panicking and rushing to acquire a startup for its technology, the company began building its own algorithms internally. The results almost immediately exceeded expectations. "The benefits of AI are real," van der Does said.

Adyen is using AI for fraud detection. That has allowed the company to better leverage the large number of data points its system absorbs to make faster and more accurate decisions about people's creditworthiness. Its risk management service -- called RevenueProtect -- includes a ShoperDNA feature, which allows for real-time identification of shoppers.

With AI, Adyen has been able to expand the data points and methodology, which in turn enables much more granular examination of a person or pattern when a purchase is being made. Its Risk Engine automates transaction reviews, which reduces review times by 30%, according to the company.
Typically, such fraud detection is measured by how it limits losses. But van der Does said it's just as important to measure additional transactions that are approved.

He used the example of an Israeli software developer who works in New York and sends a purchase to Europe with a credit card issued in Israel. There's a good chance that such a transaction might be flagged or blocked. But with AI able to process more detail, it might realize that the developer is just sending flowers and the transaction is probably fine.

This way of incorporating AI fits with Adyen's solid, problem-solving approach. The company isn't trying to spin itself as some machine learning-driven wonder. Instead, it treats AI as a practical advance.

"Risk in payments is a way to raise authorization dollars," he said. "If you allow the transaction, your merchant has more revenue than [they] would have had with the old system. That is good for everyone."

Anthropic is now xAI's biggest customer with a contract worth roughly $3.1 billion a month. Google spends $800 million. Either deal can be canceled with 90 days' notice.

In August, Musk pushed engineers in a group chat for "revenue per GPU,"frustrated in part that xAI's own models can barely compete. He reportedly renamed an internal chat "Sell compute because we can't compete."

xAI is cutting or restructuring its own AI projects to match that shift. Unit chief Mike Nicolls told staff in November that the 60-person team behind the Grok Imagine image and video generator would be disbanded. OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6.

news.summary_en: OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki revealed the log-perplexity scores for models from GPT-3.5 to GPT-6 and beyond, illustrating how capabilities emerge as metrics improve. This initiative aims to establish a common industry performance standard to encourage rivals to coordinate development pacing at critical safety thresholds.
paragraphs: OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6.

Pachocki wants to make perplexity a common measure of progress for the AI industry and published internal scores for the GPT series in a bl o g post. The metric has long been standard in AI research and Transformer development because it reliably measures how well a pretrained base model predicts the next token in a text.
Lower scores mean more accurate predictions. A perplexity of 2 roughly means the model is as uncertain about the next token as if it were choosing between two equally likely options.

Before it stopped publishing openly, OpenAI often released perplexity scores to show how its models were improving. Releasing them again is a trade-off, Pachocki writes. While rivals get a clearer picture of where OpenAI stands, he says, the need for shared safety standards outweighs that downside. He hopes for a common scientific foundation that lets labs coordinate their pace of development at critical points.
### Capabilities emerge at distinct perplexity thresholds

Pachocki says many capabilities of modern models map surprisingly closely to specific perplexity scores, even though it wasn't clear beforehand that they would appear at those thresholds. He reports the figures on a logarithmic scale called log-perplexity, where lower scores are still better. In his account, GPT-3.5 first enabled fluent conversation at around 0.99, laying the groundwork for the original ChatGPT. At about 0.91, GPT-4 unlocked productive chain-of-thought reasoning, or working through problems step by step. Below 0.8, he writes, transformative capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and math.

The published chart plots OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity by release or evaluation date through November 2026. It covers GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.2 Astra, plus an internal model at around 0.73.
### OpenAI's models deliver math breakthroughs in a Slack thread

OpenAI has been feeding its models open math problems for more than a year. Starting with a model at about 0.76 log-perplexity, the models began producing breakthrough results, Pachocki writes. For researchers with a math background, he says, it was "deeply surreal"to watch solutions to longstanding questions pop up one after another in a single Slack thread.

Those results include a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the Millennium Prize problems, though it hasn't been fully verified yet. The same goes for the proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis found by Claude and an Anthropic researcher. Pachocki thinks deep learning research itself could see something similar as soon as 2027, bringing a sudden avalanche of core advances in AI training.

A footnote says the sharp acceleration in the chart starting in 2026 comes mostly from long-term research and compute investments and less from automation. Even so, AI itself has contributed major design work on OpenAI's latest models, according to the post.

news.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
news.title_en: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
news.author: Jess Weatherbed
news.summary_en: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” desc
paragraphs: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”

“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”

The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors.

xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.
Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.

news.title: Nvidia’s About-Face on Huang Made Without Consulting Leadership
news.title_en: Nvidia’s About-Face on Huang Made Without Consulting Leadership
news.author: Zeus Kerravala
news.summary_en:
Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

paragraphs: Nvidia Corp. reported its quarterly results this week, and contrary to the prevailing narrative, the sky didn’t fall.

Revenue more than doubled year-over-year. The Vera Rubin chip platform achieved the fastest product ramp in the company’s history, and management raised its fiscal 2028 growth outlook to roughly 75%, up from 70%. By all accounts, it was a solid beat and raise.

This was Nvidia’s first earnings call without co-founder Jensen Huang, whose resignation as president and chief executive was announced on Nov. 12. Board Chair Harvey Jones told investors that the resignation followed the “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” Hours after Huang publicly said he would be willing to return, Jones said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and would not take questions about the circumstances or the board’s ongoing investigation.

Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer who is now also serving as interim CEO, set the tone in her first minute: “Our ambition will not change. Our passion for innovation will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change.”

After listening to the call, I believe Nvidia answered the short-term question and left the long-term one open. The company made a convincing case that it can execute without its founder. It has yet to show who decides where it goes next. Here are five things we learned and what they mean for those who buy, budget for or operate artificial intelligence infrastructure.
### 1. The machine will run without the founder

The fear going into the call was disruption. The quarter closed before Huang’s exit, so the results can’t settle that. The guidance can, and it went up. Hyperscalers brought Vera Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell required. The roadmap is set through Vera Rubin Ultra next year and Feynman in 2028, and Kress said the supply agreements extend through the end of the decade.

She explained that the past month has been “Business as usual.” Kress added, “We’ve engaged with our customers, suppliers and partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She also noted that TSMC leadership was at Nvidia’s offices this week.

I have long held that Nvidia’s moat was never the silicon. It’s the accumulated layers of systems, software and supply chain built around it. The past week was the first real test of that view, and so far, it’s holding. A yearly product cadence this complex runs on thousands of engineers and a supply chain planned years in advance.

Asked about talent retention, Kress acknowledged that “there are diverse opinions” among employees while insisting they are “committed to doing their life’s work” at Nvidia. The company’s talent can’t be overstated, and although Huang was the face of the company, the employees are what made it tick.

Earlier this week, Cisco Systems Inc. CEO Chuck Robbins appeared with Brian Sozzi. When asked whether he still trusts Nvidia, Robbins replied immediately, “Absolutely.” He added, “The industry’s bigger than one person. I don’t care how good you are. There are a lot of smart people. There are 42,000 people at Nvidia. So I’m not all that concerned.” Huang may have been the most visible Nvidia employee, but the company is full of smart, driven people. Leadership understands this, and I expect turnover to have minimal impact.

Employee retention is a top-of-mind issue for Nvidia executives. Business Insider reported this week that the company held its first all-hands meeting after Huang. The article noted that Kress announced plans to accelerate pay raises and equity grants, Jones discussed the CEO search and Buck outlined the roadmap. It’s reasonable to believe that Huang’s departure was a shock to employees, but the business goes on, and I expect things to settle down in short order.

paragraphs: Jensen Huang is back, baby, and Wall Street is thrilled.

The chipmaker’s shares have surged more than 30 percent following the board’s announcement that it was reinstating Huang as president, CEO and board member. The company’s valuation has soared by more than $1 trillion, which puts it on track to break Microsoft’s record for the greatest single-day gain in market value by hundreds of billions of dollars.

Huang departed the company he helped found on November 12 amid suspected asset-kissing and allegations of extramarital affairs with employees. Each report chipped away at the company’s value, until nearly $2.2 trillion was erased over the last month.

Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said during the company’s earnings call that the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” WIRED also reported that Nvidia's board had been alarmed by Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying.”

And yet, despite all this, the board announced on Monday that it had brought Huang back—with some help from the US government. Semafor reported that, hours before Huang was reinstated, President Donald Trump dialed into the publicly traded company’s board meeting to argue for the ousted CEO’s return.

Many questions remain unanswered. What happens at the conclusion of the board-led investigation into Huang’s behavior? Multiple government agencies and lawmakers are reportedly investigating Huang; given the Trump administration’s aggressive support of the executive, what sort of accountability can anyone reasonably expect?

The turmoil has also raised red flags about what happens when so much of the market revolves around one person at one company. Nvidia has massive sway over the wider artificial intelligence ecosystem, due to its deals with and investments in other companies. Last week, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 10 percent, in part due to Nvidia’s struggles—the index’s biggest decline since March 2020.

On Monday morning, CNBC asked Trump if Nvidia’s influence on the stock market influenced his decision to push for Huang’s return. “Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump responded.

Trump, who has worked closely with Huang during his second administration, established himself as a vocal supporter of the CEO amidst the recent chaos. Trump told The New York Times that he believed the board responded positively to his argument for Huang’s return because of the stock market dip, with the president suggesting that investors didn’t have much confidence in interim CEO Colette Kress.

“I just thought he should be running the company, and I didn’t know it was going to have this kind of an impact,” Trump told The New York Times. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it actually. The stock is up.”
According to Trump, however, his decision wasn’t guided solely by the market.
“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,” the president told CNBC. Sure!

news.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
news.title_en: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
news.author: James Donnell
news.summary_en:

paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here .

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.
“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences .

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

paragraphs: Anthropic is one of Elon Musk’s biggest competitors in artificial intelligence. It is also one of his biggest customers.

Since May, Mr. Musk’s SpaceX has made billions of dollars a month leasing computing power from its data centers to companies like Anthropic and Google. At the same time, SpaceX is developing its own A.I. products, like its chatbot Grok and A.I. agent Grok Bot.

Mr. Musk has told employees that SpaceX is falling behind in A.I. development, making it more lucrative to rent the company’s computing power out to rivals than use it to improve its own products, according to three people with knowledge of his comments.

But Mr. Musk is frustrated by the situation, the people said. In a group chat with hundreds of engineers at SpaceX’s A.I. unit, he shared data showing the company lagged competitors. And once a week, he has asked some group members to list their work in the chat to justify the use of specialized computer chips, or graphics processing units, which train A.I. systems, the people said.

In August, Mr. Musk temporarily changed the group chat name to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” according to communications viewed by The New York Times. He added a warning to employees who were not using the company’s computing resources wisely: “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.”

The tension highlights a central conflict in Mr. Musk’s A.I. push. He started an A.I. company, xAI, a year after OpenAI’s blockbuster release of ChatGPT in 2022, and has spent billions building data centers to catch up. Now, with SpaceX newly public and under pressure to show investors it can turn a profit, Mr. Musk is stuck renting much of that firepower out to the same companies he’s chasing.
That has set off a monthslong scramble for resources that has pitted the company’s ambitions — and at times even Mr. Musk’s pet projects — against its balance sheet.

The unit, renamed SpaceXSI, now generates more than half of all revenue for SpaceX, which once relied on money from government contracts to send rockets to space. SpaceX highlighted the risks of selling computing power to competitors in a prospectus before going public in June, saying the company’s data center leasing business could “create operational complexity.”

Anthropic and Google have each forged deals to lease computing power from SpaceX, with Anthropic’s valued at about $3.1 billion a month and Google’s $800 million a month. These deals could run through 2029, but could also be terminated by either party with 90 days’ notice.

Over the past few months, Anthropic has become SpaceXSI’s largest customer. Anthropic, which went public last week, has so much demand for computing power that by October, SpaceXSI needed to finish new data centers to fulfill the A.I. company’s orders, according to two people with knowledge of the work, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not permitted to speak publicly on the company’s behalf.

Representatives for SpaceX and Mr. Musk did not respond to a request for comment. Anthropic referred The Times to a portion of the company’s prospectus for its initial public offering that detailed its agreement with SpaceX.

While SpaceX has lagged rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic, Mr. Musk found an advantage in building data centers quickly. The more computing power a company has, the more powerful it can make its A.I. systems.

paragraphs: On November 12, 2026, the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) announced two operations against North Korean networks involved in cryptocurrency theft. Authorities obtained a court order to seize or freeze more than $1.2 billion from the Binance hack. They also neutralized the cloud infrastructure of FaceStealer, a deepfake manipulation campaign responsible for over $400 million in crypto theft over 18 months. These two cases illustrate different methods but the same strategy of exploiting the crypto ecosystem.

Read us on Google News In brief The DOJ obtains a court order targeting more than $1.2 billion stolen during the Binance hack. U.S. authorities and partners have already frozen over $2.7 billion of stolen crypto funds. The FBI attributes the Binance hack to the North Korean group TraderTraitor. The FaceStealer network allegedly stole over $400 million in cryptocurrencies in 18 months using social engineering and deepfake techniques. The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos related to this campaign. More than $1.2 billion targeted after the Binance hack The DOJ obtained court authorization to seize or freeze more than $1.2 billion from the Binance hack that occurred on October 29, 2026. This amount represents part of the digital assets already frozen thanks to cooperation between U.S. authorities and crypto sector actors.

According to the official Department of Justice statement, more than $2.7 billion has been frozen from loot estimated at more than $6 billion. The FBI attributes this attack to members of the North Korean army known as TraderTraitor.
Investigators continue to trace the crypto funds. Those behind the Binance hack are trying notably to launder the assets through:
They even managed to launder $430,000 using memecoins created on the NEAR protocol.
Important clarification: the court order covering $1.2 billion does not mean this sum has been definitively recovered. Freezing assets, seizing them, and possible confiscation are separate steps.

Binance states it has mobilized more than $6.34 billion in resources to cover the affected assets. In its announcement of November 12, the crypto exchange also indicated having published a new snapshot of its reserves. This financial coverage announced by the company should not be confused with the judicial recovery of stolen funds.

The second U.S. operation targets the cloud infrastructure used by FaceStealer. According to the DOJ, this North Korean campaign caused more than $400 million in crypto thefts over the last 18 months.

Once trust is established, hackers simulate a technical problem. They then offer a link or manipulation supposed to restore the meeting’s function. In reality, this purported solution installs malware on the victim’s computer.
Hackers can then steal crypto assets, hijack communication accounts, or exploit compromised computer access. Some intrusions reportedly manifested months after the initial infection.

The campaign also targets open-source software developers and maintainers. The potential goal: to access their devices and code repository accounts to prepare attacks against the software supply chain.

In this operation, the FBI seized over 900 webcam videos under a federal warrant. The agency also launched a dedicated FaceStealer space. It gathers information on the threat as well as recommendations for potentially compromised individuals.

news.summary_en:

paragraphs: Jensen Huang was reappointed as chief executive of Nvidia after President Trump set in motion several days of maneuvering to provide the company’s board with assurances that Mr. Huang was not facing criminal charges and did not pose a national security risk, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

Late last week, Mr. Trump decided he wanted to do whatever he could to help Mr. Huang get his old job back, the people said, despite concerns from his own national security agencies about Mr. Huang’s affair with a woman they believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset and who was also believed to be involved in possible illegal smuggling of Nvidia chips into China.

Over the weekend, Mr. Trump asked Vice President JD Vance to talk to Mr. Huang and work with Nvidia’s board to resolve the situation. Mr. Vance spoke privately with Mr. Huang over the weekend and helped the Nvidia board get the assurances it needed that the Trump administration did not believe that Mr. Huang himself posed a national security risk. Only a tiny handful of officials at the highest level of the government were aware of these conversations.

On Sunday night, Nvidia’s board told the administration that it would be announcing Mr. Huang’s reinstatement on Monday morning before the markets opened. The announcement included a note about a new compliance committee, intended to offer public assurance that the company was taking seriously the investigation into the possible smuggling of advanced chips. Mr. Trump was said to have been thrilled that the plan to restore Mr. Huang was executed without any leaks.

In directing Mr. Vance to engage with Mr. Huang and his peers, Mr. Trump was turning to one of the members of his administration with the strongest relationships in Silicon Valley. The vice president is close to some of Mr. Huang’s biggest supporters and admirers, such as David Sacks, the investor and co-chairman of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Mr. Sacks previously served as Mr. Trump’s key adviser on artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency issues.
Representatives for Mr. Huang and Mr. Vance declined to comment. A spokesman for Nvidia did not respond to an email seeking comment.

On Monday morning, Mr. Trump rejoiced in Nvidia’s action, saying on his social media website Truth Social that the company “made the correct and proper decision.” The president explicitly connected the reinstatement of Mr. Huang to the health of the U.S. economy.
“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Mr. Trump wrote.

Mr. Trump has sought to separate Mr. Huang from the investigations into chip smuggling that his government is pursuing. As The New York Times has previously reported, the U.S. intelligence community has collected evidence that a Chinese woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was having a secret affair with the Nvidia chief executive. But the Trump administration did not give Mr. Huang a so-called defensive briefing, a heads up that he was in a romantic relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.
The Singapore-based company that Ms. Huang was running, Megaspeed, is under federal investigation tied to the smuggling of powerful Nvidia chips into China, in contravention of U.S. export laws.

Mr. Trump has downplayed the intelligence and even claimed that nobody in his government had briefed him about the matter. In fact, advisers to Mr. Trump, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, briefed him at least twice about the national security concerns surrounding Mr. Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang admitted earlier his month to infidelities after initially casting his dealings with Ms. Huang as a business relationship. He also had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, The Times reported shortly before he resigned.

paragraphs: Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, six days after its chair said directors did not intend to bring him back.

The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, CEO and a board member, effective immediately, the company said on Monday. It followed "a series of discussions and meetings" with Huang, after which the board was satisfied with his "candor and ability to lead" the firm.
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

In reaching its decision, the board said it received input from "senior levels of the United States government," and based on that input, it is confident that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk." The statement did not name the officials involved.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," board chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain chair, and Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, continues as chief financial officer.
"I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment," Huang said in the statement. "I can't wait to get back to work."

The decision overturns the board's position from last week. "The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said on the company's November 17 earnings call, as Nvidia hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.

Hours earlier, Huang had offered to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company "and America." His comeback had drawn support from President Donald Trump and Elon Musk, even as CNBC reported that directors were not considering it.

Huang resigned on November 12 after reports of extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom U.S. officials suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. China has denied that she is a spy.

The independent directors' committee investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort "will proceed to conclusion," Nvidia said, and Huang has said he will cooperate with it.

The company also pointed to its new National Security and Export Control Committee, made up of independent directors, and said it is searching for a chief compliance officer to oversee compliance across the company. Nvidia said it will keep cooperating with government investigations and inquiries.

paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - US lawmakers from both parties offered sharp criticism on Monday of Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and said Congress must pass legislation to crack down on US chip exports to China and get answers.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to chair the Banking Committee starting in January, called the decision to reinstate Huang "reckless," adding the board still owes Congress answers about the company's compliance with US export controls.

"Jensen Huang's return only increases the urgency of passing bipartisan export control bills into law and making sure Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk," Warren said.
Nvidia did not immediately comment.
President Donald Trump on CNBC said he had pressed the Nvidia board to reinstate Huang and said he did not think the board would have acted without his action.

Last week, Huang agreed to testify before the US Senate in a public hearing, an aide to Republican US Senator Tim Scott said, as lawmakers probe allegations about Huang's ties to a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

Representative Don Bacon, a Republican, said, "Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high-end computer chips sales to China."
Huang separately agreed to a closed-door interview with three House committees, slated for December 1.
Democratic Representative Debbie Dingell said the Nvidia board "made an irresponsible decision to reinstate Jensen Huang before Congress has even heard from him."
She added, "There are serious national security questions that still need to be answered. The board must explain why it was willing to move ahead without those answers."
Republican Senator John Cornyn also questioned the board's determination. "No national security risk? Based on what?" Cornyn said on X.

Democratic Representative Richard Neal noted the Nvidia board cited "input from senior levels of the United States government" and said "this is one of the many reasons Congress needs to get answers on what exactly is going on here."

paragraphs: Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.
Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled.

And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle.
Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear.
And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one — but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first.

Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news?

Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.”

The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess.

news.title: Trump tells CNBC he spoke to Nvidia board directly about Jensen Huang
news.title_en: Trump tells CNBC he spoke to Nvidia board directly about Jensen Huang
news.author: Dan Mangan
news.summary_en:
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday morning that newly restored Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang "did nothing wrong."

Trump also told CNBC's Eamon Javers that "I think the [Nvidia] board acted really responsibly"in deciding to reinstate Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat,"Trump said in a phone interview.

paragraphs: President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday morning that newly restored Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang "did nothing wrong."
Trump also told CNBC's Eamon Javers that "I think the [Nvidia] board acted really responsibly"in deciding to reinstate Huang.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat,"Trump said in a phone interview.
"And we gave him assurance at least with everything we know, and we know a lot,"Trump said.
Trump said he spoke with Huang on Sunday night, before Nvdia's board announced his reinstatement.
"I'm very, very happy that the company had the courage and the board had the courage to do the right thing, and they suffered for two weeks, and the company suffered greatly,"the president said.

Asked if the fact that stocks broadly fell last week in the wake of Huang's resignation from Nvidia factored into his decision to push for the CEO's reinstatement, Trump said, "Probably so, but the bigger impact was the long term."
"The bigger impact was, you know, he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about,"Trump said.

news.title: Exclusive: Hours before Huang’s reinstatement, Trump called Nvidia’s board to argue for his return
news.title_en: Exclusive: Hours before Huang’s reinstatement, Trump called Nvidia’s board to argue for his return
news.author: Rohan Goswami and Shelby Talcott
news.summary_en:
US President Donald Trump had dialed into Nvidia’s board meeting to argue for Jensen Huang’s return, hours before the company reinstated the ousted CEO, according to people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board on Monday reinstated Huang, saying the company had received assurances from “senior levels of the United States government” that he posed no national security risk after carrying on an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decis
paragraphs: US President Donald Trump had dialed into Nvidia’s board meeting to argue for Jensen Huang’s return, hours before the company reinstated the ousted CEO, according to people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board on Monday reinstated Huang, saying the company had received assurances from “senior levels of the United States government” that he posed no national security risk after carrying on an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said.

Nvidia’s board met late last night, according to a person familiar with the matter, and voted unanimously. Huang’s resignation spurred an outcry from some Silicon Valley figures who called for his return. Semafor had previously reported that a faction of directors had continued to push for him to come back.

The anti-Jensen camp was dealt a blow when they learned a leading Huang replacement candidate, Arm CEO Rene Haas, had signed a new contract with Arm extending his employment until 2033, according to another person familiar with some directors’ thinking.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey Jones, who was elevated at the time of Huang’s Nov. 12 ouster to board chairman, said in a statement.

The decision comes less than two weeks after Huang stepped down under pressure, and returns Huang to the company he founded in 1993 and built into an AI giant. Huang has also been accused of having an affair with a subordinate.
Nvidia’s stock was up nearly 30% in early trading Monday, the biggest jump in more than two decades.

paragraphs: Z.ai is moving its flagship model to a loop architecture that runs some of its layers twice. With GLM-5.4, the company wants to mark the start of "Generalized Coding,"where code also generates videos, games, and CAD models.

Following OpenAI, Z.ai is introducing GLM-5.4, its first large model built on a loop transformer. While standard language models use each layer once per pass, GLM-5.4 runs a block of shared layers multiple times, refining the intermediate results from the previous pass to make the network deeper without adding parameters. OpenAI has used a similar architecture since GPT-6 Astra. According to Z.ai, the 750-billion-parameter model reaches performance comparable to models with 2 to 3 trillion parameters.

The team retrained the GLM-5 base model released in February into a loop model that runs 28 layers twice. Loop models trained from scratch have so far performed worse than models without shared weights under the same compute budget, Z.ai writes.
### Gates and shared caching keep the second pass manageable

Converting the model introduces a problem, Z.ai says. If the model simply overwrites intermediate states on each pass, activations grow sharply from round to round, leaving subsequent layers with values outside the range they were trained on.

To handle this, GLM-5.4 uses dedicated gates for each token and pass to control how much of the new output flows back into the data stream. According to Z.ai, the model builds context cautiously on the first pass and writes its changes back in full on the second. On difficult tokens, Z.ai says, the first pass steps in more strongly.

Because the second pass would otherwise double memory usage, both passes share the KV cache, the temporary memory for previously processed tokens. The second pass stores its own extra values only in a small local window. As a result, Z.ai says, the overhead compared to GLM-5.3 stays manageable even at a 1-million-token context.

To save on compute as well, the model uses sparse attention to pick the most relevant earlier tokens upfront rather than scanning the entire context every time, a standard technique. The second pass then reuses that selection from the first instead of making a new one. According to Z.ai, that yields nearly the same results as picking tokens separately on each pass. The company also says the model reaches up to 200 tokens per second off-peak and 70 to 80 tokens per second under load.
### A looped 30B test model beats its baseline with shorter reasoning chains

Before rolling out the architecture in its flagship, Z.ai tested it on models with 1, 4, 30, and 750 billion parameters. For a direct comparison, the team used a 30B model built on the same architecture as the large base model. Both versions had the same parameter count, while the loop version received about 10 percent more training compute. Its biggest gain came on the AIME25 math benchmark, where scores jumped from 19.2 to 30.4 points. Scores on the expert-level science questions in GPQA-Diamond rose from 47.6 to 56.3 points, and on the AA-LCR long-context test they climbed from 40.3 to 47.7 points. Gains were smaller at just over three points on the MMLU-Pro knowledge test and on IFBench, which tests instruction following.

Responses also got shorter, shrinking 14.9 percent on MMLU-Pro, 11.7 percent on GPQA-Diamond, and just 2 percent on AIME25. Z.ai says part of the reasoning shifts out of the output tokens and into the loop's extra computational depth.

It is still impossible to judge how well GLM-5.4 actually performs, as Z.ai has published no benchmark scores for the 750B model and the figures in its blog post come solely from the 30B test. There are no independent evaluations from groups like Artificial Analysis either.
